items.title: How to design a decision-grade pilot for agentic AI
items.summary: Agentic AI changes the nature of a technology evaluation. When an AI system only generates an answer, a person reviews the output and decides whether to use it. An agent goes further: It gathers context, selects tools, makes decisions, and executes a sequence of actions across the software development lifecycle.The central question for a pilot is therefore not whether the agent can produce an impressive result. It is: What evidence would be sufficient to authorize this agent to perform this workflow for this team?A feature checklist or a collection of successful demos cannot answer that. Leaders need evidence about end-to-end task completion, reliability, control enforcement, level of human effort, operational risk, and economics. This article presents a framework for producing that evidence and turning an agentic AI pilot into a defensible decision.Start with the decision, not the technologyA pilot should begin with the decision it is meant to support. "Evaluate agentic AI" is too broad. A usable decision names the workflow, the users, the proposed level of autonomy, the output the agent must produce, the acceptance criteria and metrics that define success, the quantified outcome the team expects, and the conditions under which it will proceed.For example: Decide whether an AI agent can diagnose selected CI/CD pipeline failures and prepare a merge request with a proposed fix that passes the pipeline’s tests and is accepted by the developer, within defined repository permissions, while reducing total resolution effort by at least 25% against the current baseline.This is more useful than "test an AI pipeline agent" because it fixes the output, the acceptance criteria, the control boundary, and the quantified outcome before anything runs.Define what happens on success, too: a limited rollout with one team, expansion to more teams, and/or a higher level of autonomy. Without an agreed next decision, a pilot drifts into an open-ended experiment.Define the proposed level of autonomyAgentic AI is not simply "autonomous" or "not autonomous." The same agent can operate at different levels of authority. A useful model for a pilot has four levels:Recommend: The agent analyzes the situation and recommends an action.Prepare: The agent creates an artifact, such as a merge request, issue, or remediation plan, but does not apply it.Execute with approval: The agent acts only after an authorized person approves.Execute within boundaries: The agent acts on its own inside a predefined scope and escalates exceptions.Test the level the team could realistically authorize. Evaluating only in recommendation mode says little about whether the agent can safely execute changes. Granting broad autonomy in an early evaluation adds risk without evidence.Autonomy should be earned. A team can start with recommendations, move to prepared changes, and consider bounded execution only after the agent has shown sufficient reliability and control compliance.Evaluate the workflow, not the responseTraditional model evaluation focuses on response quality. Agentic evaluation must focus on completing an end-to-end task.Take an agent that helps resolve a failed pipeline. A plausible explanation is not the outcome. The workflow may require the agent to:Identify the relevant job and logs, and separate the root cause from secondary symptoms.Inspect the right configuration and code, and propose a valid correction without unrelated changes.Create a reviewable artifact and trigger the correct validation steps.Escalate when confidence or authorization is insufficient.Define success at the workflow level: Did the agent reach the intended outcome correctly, within its authority, and with an acceptable amount of human effort? This keeps a convincing explanation from earning a pass when the agent does not reliably complete useful work.Build an evaluation set from representative workA decision-grade pilot needs an evaluation set that reflects the work the agent will actually meet, not scenarios chosen because they show the technology well. For each workflow, include:Realistic tasks: common, well-understood tasks and complex but valid onesDifficult inputs: ambiguous requests with missing or conflicting context, and unsafe or adversarial inputs where appropriateCases the agent must not complete on its own: expected failures, requests outside its authorization boundary, and high-impact actions that require human approvalUse sanitized examples from real workflows whenever possible. Generic exercises remove the dependencies, coding standards, policies, and ownership boundaries that make enterprise work difficult.Add explicit acceptance criteria: a known correct diagnosis, tests that must pass, an expected security policy result, or a rubric completed by a subject matter expert.
